claims.text: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction can track oxide phase formation and transformation as a function of time and temperature during high-temperature oxidation.
Thermogravimetric analysis provides quantitative mass-gain data that represent oxidation kinetics.
Combining HT-XRD with TGA enables simultaneous real-time tracking of oxide phase evolution and oxidation kinetics.
The starting material may be a metallic or ceramic alloy.
The alloy should initially be in a well-defined, single-phase solid-solution state.
The alloy is exposed to controlled high-temperature oxidizing conditions while being monitored by HT-XRD and TGA.
A temperature range of 800°C to 1400°C is suitable for the proposed measurements.
Air or a controlled oxygen atmosphere can be used to mimic accelerated or service-like oxidation conditions.
Oxidation at elevated temperature produces phase formation or transformation.
Changes in HT-XRD diffraction patterns reveal the formation and evolution of oxide phases.
TGA mass gain can be directly correlated with oxide-phase development observed by HT-XRD.
The combined measurements provide a more comprehensive account of microstructural evolution during oxidation than either measurement alone.
The method will produce a direct, time-resolved correlation between protective or non-protective oxide-layer growth and mass gain.
Time-resolved HT-XRD measurements can improve understanding of phase stability and oxidation behavior.
Traditional ex situ methods measure only final oxide thickness or post-exposure phase composition and do not capture dynamic oxidation.
HT-XRD time resolution may be inadequate for rapid phase transformations.
Maintaining controlled atmospheres may be difficult at very high temperatures.
Oxidation kinetics and phase-transformation resolution may require calibration and vary among alloy systems.
Post-quench XRD and SEM/EDS can be used to validate the phases identified by the in situ measurements.
